title: JPMorgan cut off lending to Situational Awareness after AI debacle - FT - TradingView
content: JPMorgan JPM ended its lending activity for Leopold Aschenbrenner’s hedge fund Situational Awareness after the investor suffered severe losses in July. JPMorgan was one of the prime lenders to Situational Awareness through its prime brokerage. After the losses were disclosed, the bank informed the hedge fund that it would terminate their lending relationship, according to a  Financial Times report on Friday, which cited people familiar with the matter. JPMorgan and Situational Awareness declined to comment to the FT. Situational Awareness has recently started working with specialist brokerage Clear Street, according to the report. Clear Street declined to comment to the FT. The news comes after CNBC reported earlier Friday that Situational Awareness, the artificial-intelligence-focused hedge fund founded by former OpenAI researcher Aschenbrenner, is again active in the markets through call option buying. Situational Awareness has been buying options positions in stocks including Advanced Micro Devices AMD, Bloom Energy (BE), Coreweave (CRWV), SK Hynix (SKHY), and Sandisk (SNDK), CNBC's David Faber reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The moves were made last week and early this week. Aschenbrenner's latest moves come after Situational Awareness sold a large portion of its public-equity portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel after suffering steep losses during a recent technology sell-off in late July. title: JPMorgan Tweaks Hims & Hers Stock Outlook on Key Risk - TradingView
content: Hims & Hers Health HIMS faces a more complicated growth path as regulatory pressure reshapes its weight-loss business, prompting JPMorgan to resume coverage at Neutral with a $32 price target. The target implies roughly 17% upside from the Sept. 10 close, but the bank wants clearer evidence that Hims can successfully transition from compounded GLP-1 drugs toward branded treatments without sacrificing margins. Hims & Hers operates a direct-to-consumer telehealth platform offering treatments across weight loss, sexual health, dermatology, mental health and other categories. The company generates revenue primarily through subscriptions and prescription medications delivered through its digital platform. JPMorgan JPM analyst Brian Smilek had previously rated the shares Overweight before coverage was suspended in June. While he remains constructive on Hims' vertical integration and expansion into new specialties and international markets, he said, "we look for execution across the strategic transition toward branded GLP-1s, durability of growth across newer specialties, deeper international penetration, and durable margin expansion." The biggest near-term challenge is weight-loss economics. Greater FDA scrutiny has constrained Hims' compounded GLP-1 business, forcing the company to lean more heavily on branded medications. Its partnership with Novo Nordisk NVO, which gives customers access to Wegovy and Ozempic, "should more than offset compounded GLP-1 headwinds," Smilek said. Hims also offers Eli Lilly LLY treatments including Zepbound and Foundayo. The tradeoff is profitability. JPMorgan warned that "near-term adjusted EBITDA margins face headwinds from the mix shift toward branded GLP-1s," because branded medicines generally offer less attractive economics than compounded products. The central question is whether Hims can replace lost compounded-GLP-1 economics with enough branded-drug volume and growth elsewhere to preserve its earnings trajectory. Investors should monitor branded GLP-1 adoption, adjusted EBITDA margins and growth across newer specialties and international markets. Success in those areas would strengthen the case that Hims is becoming a broader healthcare platform rather than relying heavily on compounded weight-loss drugs. JPMorgan also sees peptides as another potential growth opportunity. But until Hims proves the transition can support both revenue growth and durable margin expansion, the $32 target suggests upside may remain constrained by execution risk. title: JPMorgan Resets Adobe Target On Key Reason - TradingView
content: Adobe ADBE shares came under pressure after JPMorgan JPM cut its price target to $315 from $340, arguing that the software giant still needs to prove its rapidly expanding AI user base can translate into stronger revenue growth. Analyst Arti Vula maintained a Buy rating, however, pointing to Adobe's depressed valuation and potentially significant upside if monetization finally accelerates. Adobe reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $6.76 billion, up 12.8% from a year earlier and ahead of the $6.69 billion consensus estimate. Adjusted earnings of $6.13 per share also topped expectations of $6.08. Annual recurring revenue reached $27.5 billion, rising 11.2%, while free cash flow totaled $2.44 billion. Adobe modestly increased its full-year revenue and earnings outlook, although its fourth-quarter revenue forecast came in slightly below Wall Street expectations. Adobe's AI-first ARR surged 150% to more than $650 million, while Creative freemium monthly active users climbed 70% to over 100 million. Acrobat AI Assistant users doubled sequentially, and ending ARR from the Firefly app and credit packs rose 40% from the previous quarter. Yet Vula sees a gap between engagement and monetization. Remaining performance obligations increased just 8%, current RPO rose 9%, and Adobe still expects fiscal-2026 net new ARR to decline from last year. The company has also deferred some Creative Cloud pricing actions while prioritizing user acquisition and engagement. Adobe's investment case increasingly hinges on converting its enormous AI funnel into paying customers. The most important metrics are AI-first ARR growth, net new ARR, RPO growth and conversion of more than 100 million Creative freemium users into paid subscriptions. Investors should also watch whether Adobe eventually resumes pricing actions without damaging engagement. JPMorgan's bullish argument rests partly on valuation. Vula estimates Adobe trades at roughly eight times 2027 unlevered free cash flow, leaving a relatively low hurdle for upside if monetization improves. Continued strong engagement without corresponding ARR acceleration, however, could keep pressure on both earnings expectations and the stock's valuation multiple. We at StockStory place the most emphasis on long-term growth, but within financials, a stretched historical view may miss recent interest rate changes, market returns, and industry trends. JPMorgan Chase's recent performance shows its demand has slowed as its annualized revenue growth of 7.8% over the last two years was below its five-year trend. We're wary when companies in the sector see decelerations in revenue growth, as it could signal changing consumer tastes aided by low switching costs. The net interest margin (NIM) is a key profitability indicator that measures the difference between what a bank earns on its loans and what it pays on its deposits. This metric measures how efficiently it can generate income from its core lending activities. Over the past two years, we can see that JPMorgan Chase's net interest margin averaged a poor 2.5%. This metric is well below other banks, signaling its loans aren't very profitable. Topline growth alone doesn't tell the complete story — the profitability of that growth shapes actual earnings impact. Banks track this dynamic through efficiency ratios, which compare non-interest expenses such as personnel, rent, IT, and marketing costs to total revenue streams. Markets understand that a bank's expense base depends on its revenue mix and what mostly drives share price performance is the change in this ratio, rather than its absolute value. It's somewhat counterintuitive, but a lower efficiency ratio is better. For the next 12 months, Wall Street expects JPMorgan Chase to become less profitable as it anticipates an efficiency ratio of 52.8% compared to 50.7% over the past year. JPMorgan's JPM move to expand corporate banking into Greece adds another leg to its broader European growth strategy. By targeting large and mid-sized companies with lending, financing, hedging and investment banking (IB) services, the bank is positioning itself to deepen client relationships and capture a larger share of the corporate wallet.The expansion also builds on JPMorgan's recent investment in the region, including a 25% increase in global corporate banking staff across Europe, the Middle East and Africa over the past two years, underscoring its focus on gaining scale and market share across EMEA.The Greece expansion could strengthen JPMorgan's revenue opportunity by widening its corporate client base and creating more scope for cross-selling. Beyond traditional lending, the bank can deepen relationships through treasury, payments, liquidity management, risk solutions and IB services. That broader product mix should help JPMorgan generate both net interest income and fee revenues from the same corporate relationships, supporting more diversified growth over time.JPMorgan has been building its Greek franchise for several years. In 2022, it announced plans for a new Athens office and a Payments Innovation Lab, initially targeting around 50 hires focused on payments technology, distributed-ledger technology, artificial intelligence and cryptography. The bank's presence in Greece dates back to 1968, and it already provides IB, payments and asset-management services to Greek clients. Separately, JPMorgan consolidated much of its European Union client-facing operations into J.P. Morgan SE in 2022, creating a more scalable structure for serving customers across the region.For JPMorgan, Greece alone is unlikely to materially impact near-term results, given the bank's enormous global scale. However, the expansion is strategically positive. Adding corporate relationships in a growing economy can support loan balances, payments activity, advisory fees and capital-markets revenues over time, while JPMorgan's existing European infrastructure should provide operating leverage as the business scales. JPM's two close peers, Citigroup C and Bank of America BAC, have also been strengthening their international corporate-banking capabilities in ways that echo JPMorgan's broader EMEA push.Citigroup continues to lean on its global network to deepen relationships with multinational and institutional clients. In 2025, Citigroup expanded its Token Services platform to Dublin and added euro-denominated transactions, improving 24/7 cross-border liquidity and payment capabilities for corporate clients. More recently, the bank strengthened leadership across its Middle East and Africa franchise, where it operates across 59 markets, reinforcing its focus on cross-border banking, client connectivity and regional growth.Bank of America has likewise been investing in its global corporate-banking platform, particularly through payments and treasury services. In June 2026, the bank announced plans to launch a cross-border real-time payments solution for corporate, commercial and financial-institution clients, extending the capabilities of its CashPro platform. The effort complements Bank of America's already strong European corporate-banking franchise and could help it capture more payment flows, deepen client engagement and support fee growth. Over the past six months, JPM shares have gained 25% compared with the industry's 27.2% growth. From a valuation standpoint, JPMorgan trades at a 12-month trailing price-to-tangible book (P/TB) of 3.29X, slightly below the industry average. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for JPMorgan's 2026 earnings suggests a 22.7% rise on a year-over-year basis, while 2027 earnings are expected to grow at a rate of 0.3%. title: Vertex trades higher after JPM gives bullish rating - TradingView
content: Vertex Pharmaceuticals VRTX stock rose 1.6% premarket on Friday after J.P. Morgan moved to an Overweight rating for the company. The brokerage also set a December 2027 price target of $560 for the stock, implying an upside of nearly 9% to the last close. “Despite a full clinical pipeline poised to build upon growth from its market-leading cystic fibrosis franchise, Vertex continues to expand its breadth with the recent Crinetics acquisition adding a fifth pillar, this time in endocrinology. We expect immediate topline contribution from Palsonify, and, in time, atumelnant, to make the deal accretive to operating income by 2029,” said J.P. Morgan analyst Jessica Fye. Earlier in July, Vertex, well known for its cystic fibrosis franchise, completed the $10B transaction, adding Crinetics’ lead product, Palsonify, which is indicated in the U.S. for adults with acromegaly, a rare hormonal disorder affecting an estimated 20K Americans. “Crinetics also brings a broad early-stage pipeline and what we view as an effective small-molecule discovery engine. As true specialty products, we see these assets fitting well within VRTX’s commercial model. Following healthy 2Q sales of $24mm, we model Palsonify delivering just north of $500mm in 2030 revs and see multi-billion dollar potential for atumelnant,” added Fye. Fye also said that the investment firm expects VRTX’s core CF products Trikafta/Alyftrek to enjoy a long runway without meaningful competition. Morgan Stanley, in September, also resumed its coverage with an Overweight recommendation and a $665 per share target on Vertex, citing diversification benefits from the company’s acquisition of Crinetics Pharmaceuticals. title: Heron Power Secures $60 Million Credit Facility From J.P. Morgan And TriplePoint Capital, Adds Zach Kirkhorn To Board - Pulse 2.0
content: Heron Power has secured a $60 million credit facility from J.P. Morgan and TriplePoint Capital as the advanced power electronics manufacturer prepares to move from engineering into large-scale production. The company also appointed former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn to its board of directors. The financing follows Heron’s $140 million Series B, which closed in February 2026 and was co-led by Andreessen Horowitz’s American Dynamism Fund and Breakthrough Energy Ventures. Heron is converting a 286,000-square-foot facility in Morgan Hill, California, into Heron Factory One, with mass production targeted to begin in late 2027. The company said it has identified more than 40 gigawatts of customer interest in Heron Link, its 5-megawatt medium-voltage power conversion system. Heron Link is designed to allow renewable energy, battery storage and data center developers to connect directly to medium-voltage transmission without a transformer. Heron combines power electronics, software and high-volume manufacturing to develop infrastructure intended to help electricity systems add capacity more quickly and reliably. Kirkhorn has invested in Heron since its Series A in 2025 and has advised the company on financial and operational matters. He spent 13 years at Tesla and served as CFO during the automaker’s first full year of profitability and the expansion of its vehicle and battery manufacturing footprint across North America, Europe and Asia. “A strong balance sheet and bench of advisors is key as we move from engineering to scale. Our customers plan projects years in advance and need a dependable power conversion partner. By adding Zach to the board, we benefit from his hard-won wisdom navigating the challenging path from 1 delivered unit to profitability.” “Having been with Heron since nearly the beginning, as an investor and advisor, I’ve seen firsthand the exceptional capability, experience, and pace of execution of this team. Modernizing the grid and reducing the cost of delivering power is one of our most important industrial challenges. It’s terrific to be working with Drew again and an honor to support the team as a member of the board.” “Heron Power is addressing a key bottleneck in the modern grid: scaling next-generation power electronics that can support faster deployment and reliability as demand grows. J.P Morgan is proud to support Heron’s next phase of growth as the company prepares to ramp manufacturing.” Julia Grinshpun, Managing Director, Climate Tech at J.P. title: $100 oil isn’t as scary as it used to be - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. $100 oil has historically been met with stock market selloffs, a spike in bond yields and uncertainty around the economy. But unlike prior episodes—where triple-digit oil prices triggered worries around growth, inflation and the reaction in financial markets—Brent crude’s most recent foray above the $100 per barrel mark has wreaked less havoc than usual.

The S&P 500 sits within range of an all-time high, which stands in stark contrast to the initial shock around escalating Middle East tensions earlier this year and triggered a sharp repricing across financial markets. This time around, investors are not reacting to the headline price of oil, but rather the economic signal embedded within it. Today, that signal is far less alarming than $100 oil would traditionally suggest. Oil prices have largely fluctuated between $80 and $100 per barrel over the last few months, but the largest pressure point remains in crude products. Even with growing refining margins, and gasoline prices averaging above $4 per gallon since the conflict in Iran began, consumers have been able to weather the higher prices.

As a percentage of disposable income, gasoline expenditure only sits at about 2.5%—one of the lowest levels in the past 65 years. After several rounds of fiscal stimulus, tariff refunds and tax cuts, households have largely deleveraged to multi-decade lows, creating a larger buffer against higher prices. That better positions them relative to the oil shocks of the 1970s, the commodity boom of the mid-2000s or even the 2022 inflation spike after the war in Ukraine began. The same gasoline price increase that would have meaningfully squeezed household budgets two decades ago, or even four years ago, now represents a materially smaller drag on spending power. That doesn’t mean higher energy costs are irrelevant. Consumers at lower-income brackets remain most vulnerable, and prolonged increases in fuel prices can eventually weigh on discretionary spending. But today's energy prices are proving to be less restrictive. As households are proving more resilient, financial markets are sending a similar message. Financial markets respond to the change in energy prices, not necessarily the level. In March and April, energy markets were forced to price a highly uncertain geopolitical event: the conflict in Iran. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz raised the possibility of a meaningful and sustained disruption to global oil supply. Brent surged from roughly $60 per barrel to nearly $120 within a matter of weeks.

At the time, investors were facing a scenario with very little visibility and the significant risk that supply losses could become structural rather than temporary. That uncertainty and the doubling of energy prices sent stocks down nearly 10%, only to recover in 11 trading days, with oil prices retracing part of their move shortly after. Even as oil prices have moved higher, investors are no longer pricing a worst-case disruption scenario that would inhibit the economy, and by extension the stock market. A world where oil is expensive but supply remains available is fundamentally different from one in which investors are trying to assess whether a substantial share of global production could disappear overnight. To be clear, escalation remains a risk. Direct disruption to critical energy infrastructure would likely push oil materially higher and generate a much stronger headwind for risk assets. But for now, investors are viewing oil’s rise as a function of supply constraints rather than a full-fledged energy crisis. That message is reinforced by the bond market, which isn’t behaving like a major inflation shock is unfolding. Yes, long-term yields show a building correlation with the squeeze in refined products, but they are still inching higher, not jumping higher. That does not signal a sharp repricing in interest rates that could jolt the stock market. Triple-digit oil prices still matter. They can push inflation higher, influence central bank policy and weigh on consumer sentiment. But today’s energy shock looks fundamentally different from past episodes. Consumers are spending a smaller share of their income on fuel, bond markets are not signaling a renewed inflation spiral, and investors are no longer pricing a prolonged supply disruption. The key variable is not the level of oil prices but whether higher energy costs begin to spill over into broader inflation expectations and consumer spending. So far, there is little evidence of that happening, which is why $100 oil—while uncomfortable—is simply not as scary as it once was. title: J.P. Morgan Names Nelle Miller And William Sinclair As Co-CEOs Of $2.4 Trillion U.S. Private Bank - Pulse 2.0
content: J.P. Morgan announced that Nelle Miller and William Sinclair have been appointed Co-CEOs of the U.S. Private Bank, effective immediately. Miller and Sinclair will lead J.P. Morgan’s $2.4 trillion U.S. private banking business, which includes more than 5,500 professionals across 57 offices serving individuals, families, entrepreneurs, executives, family offices, and institutions throughout the country. The U.S. Private Bank is the largest market within J.P. Morgan’s Global Private Bank, which oversees more than $3.8 trillion in client assets worldwide. The appointments follow the July 2025 appointment of David Frame as Global CEO of J.P. Morgan Private Bank and reflect the increasingly global nature of the firm’s wealthiest clients and their investments. Miller currently serves as Head of New York, the Private Bank’s largest U.S. market. She joined J.P. Morgan in 2002 and has held several leadership positions across the firm. She was a founding member of the Global Investment Opportunities team and has led national specialist groups serving complex families and institutions, including the Outsourced CIO and Morgan Private Advisory organizations. Sinclair joined J.P. Morgan in 2007 and has built one of the firm’s largest client practices, leading more than 500 professionals. He currently serves as Head of the Financial Leaders Group and Global Co-Head of the Family Office Practice, advising some of the firm’s largest and most complex clients across public and private investments, fixed-income strategies, credit and liquidity solutions, estate planning, and philanthropy. In their new roles, Miller and Sinclair will oversee J.P. Morgan’s efforts to expand its U.S. private banking franchise while connecting clients with the broader capabilities of the firm’s global platform. “The Global Private Bank has delivered strong growth over the past five years, and the U.S. is at the center of that momentum. Nelle and Will have built outstanding businesses, developed high-performing teams and demonstrated deep expertise. They are uniquely well positioned to lead the U.S. Private Bank into its next chapter.” David Frame, Global CEO of J.P. Morgan Private Bank “I have spent my career alongside clients through market cycles and the most meaningful moments in their families’ lives, and Will and I are fortunate to lead a team that knows our clients just as deeply. The decisions families face today are more interconnected than ever spanning private markets, liquidity and multigenerational planning. This is an extraordinary opportunity to build on everything that makes this business special.” Nelle Miller, Co-CEO of J.P. Morgan U.S. Private Bank “Nelle and I are honored to take on this responsibility together and bring the global scale of the Private Bank to families and markets across the U.S. We have a fantastic franchise, with exceptional people and an unparalleled breadth of capabilities. Our focus will be on delivering the full power of J.P. Morgan to our clients and continuing to attract and develop the best talent in the industry.” William Sinclair, Co-CEO of J.P. title: 5 Generational Shifts Reshaping Family Wealth Planning Today - J.P. Morgan

From supporting adult children to hiring health concierges, broad societal changes are changing how some families think about wealth management. Here’s how to adapt to today’s shifting landscape. Executive Director, National Lead for Outsourced Family Office, J.P. Morgan Wealth Management Imagine, for a moment, a fictional family gathering for a weekend getaway for a milestone birthday. In this hypothetical scenario, the Parkers spend the evening at a favorite restaurant for a few hours together before everyone scatters back to their busy lives. But over coffee the next morning, the conversation turns from strictly celebratory to tactical. A daughter asks whether “help with a home” is possible given today’s market. A son wonders, candidly, what the family’s long-term financial plan actually is – and who is in charge of it. Their parents, in turn, share something they’ve never said out loud: They feel responsible not just for financial outcomes, but for defining the family culture that will shape those outcomes long after they’re gone. It’s a sentiment we see among some of the families we work with every day, who are trying to figure out the best financial structures for their household amid broader societal changes like the rising cost of living and later marriage timelines. It is imperative for families to understand these shifts so that they can anticipate pain points ahead and get a jump on addressing them. Below, we take a closer look at some of the issues we’re seeing more often with clients and break down what you need to know about each of these concepts, from supporting adult children to coordinating healthcare. Young adults today face a vastly different economic landscape than the one from a decade or more ago. From housing to food, they can expect to spend much more than prior generations did, leading to possible life launch delays (e.g., buying a home or starting a family later in life).1 Some families are more prepared to give aid than they were in the past, viewing it as necessary in today’s economy. These parents and grandparents understand that the rules of the game have changed since they were young adults. While this support can provide helpful financial stability, it can also be sporadic and unstructured, leading to sibling comparisons, blurred boundaries and confusion about whether the support is a one-time offer or ongoing investment. Most crucially, objectivity matters. Parents and grandparents will want to ensure that consistent governance processes are followed for each heir, and that decisions aren’t driven by personality, but by principle. As the world becomes more fragmented, some families are turning to their values as an anchor across generations, focusing on planning within an ethical framework. Part of that includes values statements, which help family office clients codify who they are, how they intend their heirs to behave with the money and the impact they hope their wealth will have on the world. This focus on purpose is often embodied in their charitable planning. Families may create charitable entities and name specific causes that those entities support. They may even mandate all family member involvement in these causes to ensure adherence to established ethical principles. These endeavors provide an accessible entry point for younger generations to learn about wealth deployment as they are given the opportunity to select organizations that align with their family values. This can be a tremendous benefit to family members in the next generation, as they learn the discernment and shared decision making it takes to be sound stewards of the family’s wealth in a relatively safe setting. Modern-day families are navigating new financial and communication dynamics along with greater global access to information, which can create evolving expectations around transparency among younger generations.

These calls for increased transparency between generations can change family dynamics. This can be positive if they are handled appropriately. Having more conversations about family wealth can make members feel valued and included. On the other hand, these talks can put pressure on parents and grandparents to share more than they planned to earlier than they intended.

J.P. Morgan Wealth Management research has found that while all generations genuinely want to “do right” by their wealth, they may avoid the topic.2  Although communication styles may differ from one generation to the next, it’s imperative to develop clear rules for sharing information and a process for including younger family members. Like the rising cost of living, there are other broad changing societal dynamics that are influencing families, including later marriages and blended families. Add business equity and other complicated financial concerns to the mix, and premarital planning can become complex.

As a result, we’re seeing more families opt for prenuptial agreements and trust protection. While one is often enough to protect assets in the event of a divorce, families often want a contingency in place. For example, in some families, an inheritance is passed on via an irrevocable trust, which should ensure that the assets are treated as nonmarital property. But a prenup may also be executed stating that any inheritance is nonmarital. These families often pay for independent counsel for their child’s soon-to-be spouse. Also, as a gesture of goodwill, some families may take additional steps to pay off the new spouse’s student loans or purchase the newlywed’s home in both of their names. These concessions can help head off potentially contentious disagreements while financially welcoming the new family members. Healthcare is also becoming a more important family-wide consideration, given the complexity and expense. Planning for medical care has no shortage of technicalities – financial and logistical. Families need to consider care navigation, patient advocacy, coverage decisions and privacy while managing costs.

To help, some families may hire concierge services for all family members that can coordinate medical providers and facilitate access to leading specialists. These concierge services ensure speed and confidence in medical decision making in times when families might be stressed or overwhelmed on their own. Modern family wealth planning is increasingly about aligning the family’s intent with the family’s lived reality. Given what we see from clients, here are a few steps to consider: The more resilient families aren’t the ones with the most complex structures – they’re the ones with the clearest shared understanding. In an era where costs are moving higher, information travels fast and expectations are evolving, the real opportunity is to be proactive – to replace ambiguity with intentional choices and to turn planning from a set of documents into a durable family operating system.
